wm-residual.why: World models learn physics from scratch, which is absurd when you already have a simulator and a robot model that are right about most of it. Giving the model that structure and learning only the residual should cut sample complexity enormously, and should produce rollouts that stay physically plausible instead of drifting into nonsense.
wm-residual.state:
The residual idea is proven at the actuator and dynamics level. [[anymal-hwangbo]]'s learned actuator network is the canonical instance — identify the real actuator's torque response from data and put that in the simulator, rather than randomizing over your ignorance. [[asap]] is the modern whole-body version: learn a delta-action model from real rollouts and fine-tune the policy against the corrected simulator. [[dexndm]] does the same joint-wise for a dexterous hand. All three are residual physics, and all three work.

The world-model side has the machinery but not the prior. [[dreamerv3]] and [[dreamerv4]] are domain-agnostic by design; [[tdmpc2]] is decoder-free and cheap; [[vjepa2]] predicts in latent space; [[pwm]] uses first-order gradients through a learned smooth model, which is the closest to a differentiable hybrid. None of them are given a simulator to start from.

And a better prior may be arriving. [[newton]] is NVIDIA, Google DeepMind and Disney Research building one GPU physics engine together, with rigid and flexible bodies in the same scene. If its contact model is materially better than MuJoCo's, the residual you need to learn gets smaller — which is the whole argument. Benchmark it rather than assuming.

Differentiable simulation is the other half. [[diff-contact-design]] and [[genesis]] make the analytic model differentiable, which is what you need if the residual is to be trained end to end against the prior.
threads: Residual dynamics. [[anymal-hwangbo]], [[asap]], [[dexndm]]. Read all three; they are the same idea at three scales.
Latent world models. [[dreamerv3]], [[dreamerv4]], [[tdmpc2]], [[vjepa2]].
Differentiable physics. [[genesis]], [[diff-contact-design]], [[pwm]].
Auxiliary-loss world modelling. [[flare]] — the cheap way to test whether the prior helps.
wm-residual.gap:
Nobody has built a world model whose backbone is a simulator. The residual-physics literature corrects a simulator to help a policy; the world-model literature learns dynamics from scratch. The hybrid — roll out MuJoCo, predict the residual with a learned model, and train the agent inside the sum — is an obvious construction that has not been done for robot manipulation.

The claim to test is sharp and falsifiable: sample complexity versus a pure learned world model, at matched final performance. And a second one that matters more for safety — rollouts from a physics-backed model should stay plausible for far longer horizons, which you can measure directly as divergence from ground truth over time.
plan:
Pick a task where the analytic model is good but not perfect: contact-rich insertion, or in-hand
  rotation. Free-space reaching will not show anything.
Implement the baseline pure world model ([[tdmpc2]] is cheapest) and the sim-only baseline. You need both.

Add the residual: MuJoCo rollout plus a learned correction on the state delta, trained on real or
  higher-fidelity rollouts. This is exactly [[asap]]'s delta-action model used as a dynamics model rather
  than an action corrector.
Headline figure: sample complexity to a fixed success rate, three ways.
Second figure: rollout divergence versus horizon length. This is where physics-backed should win big.
risks: The residual absorbs everything. If it is high-capacity it will just learn the dynamics and you are back where you started. Constrain capacity and report what fraction of the prediction the prior explains.
Differentiating through contact is unstable. Well known. Consider keeping the prior non-differentiable and training the residual on rollouts instead.
The prior is wrong in the regime you care about. Contact is exactly where simulators are weakest, which is both the risk and the reason the experiment is interesting.

read.why: The delta-action model. This is your residual, already built and validated — repurpose it as a dynamics model.
The original residual-physics argument, and still the clearest.
The dexterous-hand version: joint-wise learned dynamics closing the reality gap.
The cheapest pure world-model baseline to beat.
Latent prediction, for the architecture of the learned half.
The cheap first experiment before building anything.
First-order gradients through a learned smooth model, if you want it differentiable end to end.
The new joint NVIDIA/DeepMind/Disney physics engine — a better prior means a smaller residual.
The opposite bet: skip the prior and let a video world model generate the data.

auto-research-wm.why: Real-robot experiments are the scarce resource. If an agent can form hypotheses, test them inside a learned world model, and spend physical robot time only on the survivors, the throughput of a lab changes qualitatively rather than incrementally.
auto-research-wm.state:
Training agents entirely inside a world model now works. [[dreamerv4]] learns Minecraft diamonds from offline data alone by training the agent purely in imagination — which is the strongest existing signal that a learned model can substitute for interaction. [[genie3]] generates interactive worlds in real time with minute-scale consistency. [[dreamerv3]] established that one hyperparameter set works across 150+ domains.

The agentic research loop exists separately. [[ai-scientist]] and [[agent-laboratory]] run the hypothesis-to-paper loop; [[eureka]] and [[rf-agent]] run the narrower reward-design loop with actual training in it; [[harbor]] automates the robot RL workflow; [[real-deep-research]] does agentic analysis of the literature itself.

And the world model is already being used as a data engine, which is one step short of this idea. [[dreamgen]] generates trajectories for behaviours the robot has never performed and trains on them; [[robocurate]] verifies they are executable first. Substitute "hypotheses" for "trajectories" and you have the loop you are proposing.

What is missing is the join. Nobody uses a learned world model as the cheap experiment substrate for an agent that is doing research. The two literatures do not cite each other.
threads: Agents inside world models. [[dreamerv4]], [[genie3]], [[dreamerv3]].
Agentic experiment loops. [[eureka]], [[rf-agent]], [[harbor]], [[ai-scientist]].
Self-improvement. [[robocat]], [[voyager]], [[pld]].
Model fidelity as the gating variable. [[asap]], [[dexndm]] — how wrong the model is determines whether any of this is sound.
auto-research-wm.gap:
The join is the contribution, and it has a sharp, testable form: does hypothesis triage inside a learned world model actually save real-robot time? Run the agent loop twice — once with every hypothesis tested on hardware, once with the world model filtering first — and report robot-hours to reach the same conclusion.

The failure mode is well defined too, and worth measuring: the model's false-negative rate. A world model that confidently rejects a hypothesis that would have worked is worse than no filter at all, and nobody has quantified that for robot dynamics.
plan:
Start narrow. One task family, one world model ([[tdmpc2]] or [[flare]]-style), a hypothesis space of
  reward and controller variants rather than open-ended ideas.

Calibrate the model before trusting it: rank 20 known-outcome variants in the model and compare with
  their real ranking. That correlation is the gating result — if it is weak, stop.
Then the triage experiment: robot-hours to a fixed conclusion, with and without model filtering.
Report false negatives explicitly. This is the number that decides whether anyone should use this.
Use [[harbor]] for orchestration and the physical harness for the real-robot arm of the comparison.
risks: Model error is correlated with what is interesting. Novel hypotheses are exactly the ones the model has least data on. This is a real and possibly fatal objection — confront it in the calibration step.
Compounding automation error. An agent on top of a world model on top of a simulator is three layers of approximation. Keep the hypothesis space narrow.
It becomes an LLM paper. Keep the contribution measured in robot-hours saved, not in prompt design.

The orchestration layer, already built for robot RL.
The narrow version of the loop that demonstrably works.
What interactive world generation now looks like.
The honest limits of agent-run research — read the criticism too.
How wrong your model is, and how to make it less wrong.
The world model already used as a generator of things that never happened — one step from hypothesis testing.
Verifying what the model generated is physically real. The credibility step.

third-person.why: Third-person human video is the single most abundant demonstration source that exists — every cooking video, every assembly tutorial, every sports clip. It is also the hardest to use, because you have both an embodiment gap and a viewpoint gap at once, and the viewpoint gap changes with every clip.
third-person.state:
The paired data now exists. [[egoexo4d]] gives time-synchronized first- and third-person video of the same skilled activity, which turns "is ego better than exo?" from an argument into an experiment. That dataset is the reason this idea is tractable now and was not three years ago.

Representation transfer works from either viewpoint. [[r3m]] pretrains on Ego4D and cuts robot demonstrations by roughly an order of magnitude; [[vip]] extracts a dense reward. Neither is viewpoint-specific.

Action transfer is where viewpoint bites. [[mimicplay]] uses human play video for the high-level planner and a small amount of teleop for the low-level controller — a sensible division that sidesteps the viewpoint problem by only asking the video for coarse information. [[vid2robot]] conditions the policy on a human video of the task instead of a language string. [[x-mimicfuncimitatingtoolmanipulationfromas]] imitates tool manipulation from a single human video via functional correspondence.

Pixel editing works from third person too. [[phantom]] edits the human out and paints the robot in, training with zero robot demonstrations — and that approach is largely viewpoint-agnostic, which makes it a surprisingly strong baseline here.

And viewpoint robustness has its own line now. [[egodemogen]] synthesises novel egocentric views; the same trick applies to exocentric capture.
threads: Paired ego/exo data. [[egoexo4d]] — the substrate for any honest comparison.
Viewpoint-agnostic representations. [[r3m]], [[vip]], [[vjepa2]].
Coarse-from-video, fine-from-teleop. [[mimicplay]]. The most robust practical split.
Video-conditioned policies. [[vid2robot]], [[x-mimicfuncimitatingtoolmanipulationfromas]].
Pixel editing. [[phantom]] — works from either viewpoint.
View augmentation. [[egodemogen]], [[one-demo]].
third-person.gap:
The field has quietly assumed egocentric is better, because it matches the robot's wrist camera, and has mostly stopped asking. But third-person video is far more abundant, and [[egoexo4d]] makes the comparison runnable. The unclaimed result is the controlled ego-versus-exo study: same task, same paired data, same policy class, varying only viewpoint — and reported per task type, because the answer is almost certainly "ego for fine manipulation, exo for anything involving the whole body or the scene layout".

That finding would be immediately useful to everyone building capture rigs, and it is a study rather than a system, which makes it fast.
plan: Use [[egoexo4d]] directly. The paired structure is the entire reason this is cheap.
Fix everything but viewpoint: one policy class, one pretraining recipe, one task set.
Run three arms: ego-only, exo-only, both. Report per task category.

Add [[phantom]]-style editing as a fourth arm, since it should be the most viewpoint-robust and nobody
  has checked that claim.
Close with the practical recommendation — which viewpoint to buy a camera for, given a task type.
risks: Confounds in the dataset. Ego and exo clips differ in resolution, motion blur and framing as well as viewpoint. Control for what you can and report what you cannot.
The answer is boring. "It depends on the task" is the likely result — which is fine if the dependence is characterised precisely enough to act on.
Someone runs it first. It is an obvious study. Move quickly or scope to dexterous tasks where you have the hardware advantage.

Conditioning the policy on a human video rather than a language string.
Single human video to tool manipulation via functional correspondence.
The 2026 map of the area — position against it explicitly.

hri-collab.why: Physical collaboration with a person is the hardest case of the M2 problem: your partner's policy is unknown, non-stationary, and cannot be retrained. It is also the case with the clearest path to something people actually want, since most useful physical tasks in a home or a workshop involve a human.
hri-collab.state:
Humanoid co-manipulation has a concrete recent instance. [[h2compact]] does human-humanoid co-manipulation with adaptive contact trajectory policies — in your own M2 library. The related work in your collaborative_transport folder (carbon-fibre plies, co-manipulated systems, human-guided transport) covers the industrial side.

Force-adaptive whole-body control is the enabling capability. [[falcon]]'s decoupled upper/lower-body formulation with an explicit external-force curriculum is exactly what a robot carrying one end of something with a person needs, and it is directly portable to MABEL.

Intent prediction now has purpose-built data and a sharper framing. [[interact]] predicts human intent conditioned on what the robot is doing — most datasets treat the human as if the robot were not there, which is precisely the assumption that fails in collaboration. [[intention-tracking]] adds a hierarchical version that both avoids interrupting the human and intervenes when the human is failing, and [[workspace-opt]] makes the genuinely contrarian move of arranging the workspace so the human moves more predictably instead of modelling the variance. On the data side, Kaiwu records human, environment and robot synchronously, and MoGaze pairs full-body motion with workspace geometry and eye gaze — see the Datasets tab.

Intent inference is the part borrowed from elsewhere. The MARL literature's opponent modelling ([[mappo]] and the belief-based opponent-shaping work in your library) is the formal version of "guess what your partner is about to do", and human-video work ([[r3m]], [[vip]]) is where the perception side comes from.

And corrections-as-data is the loop that makes it improve. [[hil-serl]] and [[pi06]] both treat human intervention as a first-class training signal rather than a nuisance.
threads: Physical human-robot co-manipulation. [[h2compact]], and the co-manipulation papers in your M2 collaborative_transport folder.
Force-adaptive control. [[falcon]], [[deep-wbc]].
Intent inference. Opponent modelling from MARL, adapted to a partner you cannot train.
Corrections as data. [[hil-serl]], [[pi06]].
Handovers. The task-oriented handover work in your whole_body_loco_manipulation folder.
hri-collab.gap:
The measurement is missing. Physical HRI papers report task success and occasionally a subjective comfort survey. What they do not report is who is doing the adapting. In almost every deployed system the human silently adapts to the robot, and the paper claims the collaboration worked.

The data to do it now exists — Kaiwu records all three streams at once, MoGaze gives gaze as an early intent signal, and [[interact]] provides the robot-conditioned framing — so this is a study you could run rather than a dataset you would first have to build.

An experiment that quantifies the division of adaptation — how much the human's trajectory changes when partnered with the robot versus with another human, on the same task — would be a genuinely novel measurement, and it is the one that distinguishes a collaborative robot from a compliant one. It connects directly to M2, where you already have the two-agent infrastructure and can substitute a human for one agent.
plan:
Reuse the M2 collaborative-transport setup with a human replacing one robot. The instrumentation is
  already there.

Collect the human-human baseline on the same task. Without it there is nothing to compare against, and
  this is the step everyone skips.

Measure adaptation on both sides: trajectory deviation from solo behaviour, internal force, lead/follow
  switching frequency.

Then intervene: give the robot an intent-inference module and show the human's adaptation burden drops.
  That is the result.
Report the subjective measures too, but lead with the objective ones.
risks: Human-subject approval and variance. Budget time for ethics approval and enough participants for the variance, which will be large.
Safety. A force-adaptive whole-body controller sharing a payload with a person needs a real safety case, not a software limit.
The human adapts anyway. People are extremely good at compensating. Designing a task where that compensation is measurable rather than invisible is the hard experimental-design problem.

The force-adaptive whole-body control this needs underneath.
The formal frame for reasoning about a partner whose policy you do not control.
Human corrections as a first-class training signal.
The same idea at scale — interventions during autonomous execution.
Human intent predicted conditioned on the robot's actions — the framing most datasets miss.
Assistive intervention, not just collision avoidance. The behaviour that makes a collaborator.
Reduce the human's motion variance instead of modelling it better. Cheap and clever.
Its human-in-the-loop mode is the bridge between your multi-robot and HRI ideas.
Whole-body control with arm and legs in one policy.

soft-sim2real.why: Deformables break sim-to-real twice at once. The physics is wrong — cloth, rope and soft objects are badly modelled by every general-purpose simulator — and the rendering is wrong, because a simulated towel does not look like a real one to a CNN. Most work attacks one gap and inherits the other.
soft-sim2real.state:
The field is unusually honest about being stuck. The recent literature states plainly that widely-used simulators exhibit unreliable contact dynamics for thin structures, that demonstration-synthesis pipelines built for rigid bodies transfer poorly to deformables, and that pixel-based end-to-end policy learning for deformables has stagnated on precisely this gap. That is a refreshing starting point.

The rendering gap has recent attacks. [[simweaver]] (June 2026) claims zero-shot RGB sim-to-real for deformable manipulation. [[phantom]]'s editing approach sidesteps rendering entirely by working on real video.

The physics gap has its own line. [[real2sim]] identifies dynamics for a cable from real rollouts; [[dist-r2s2r]] does the distributional version for deformable linear objects; [[soft-gentle]] makes "do not break it" a differentiable stress-guided objective; [[genesis]] offers unified multi-material simulation (rigid, MPM, SPH, cloth), which is the main practical reason to care about it.

And the residual-physics escape hatch applies here too. [[asap]] and [[dexndm]] correct the simulator from real data rather than trying to make it right a priori, which for deformables may be the only tractable route.
threads: Rendering gap. [[simweaver]], [[phantom]]. Editing real pixels often beats matching them.
Physics gap. [[real2sim]], [[dist-r2s2r]], [[genesis]], [[soft-gentle]].
Residual correction. [[asap]], [[dexndm]] — learn the discrepancy instead of removing it.
Tactile as the missing observation. [[dexskin]], [[dream-tac]] — for deformables, contact tells you things vision cannot, and this is barely explored.
Real-to-sim loops. [[egoengine]], [[video2sim2real]] — reconstruct the specific object rather than modelling the class.
soft-sim2real.gap:
The two gaps are always attacked separately, and that is the opening. An ablation that separates them — same task, same policy, four conditions (real physics/real render, sim physics/real render via editing, real physics/sim render, sim/sim) — would tell the field which gap to spend money on. That experiment is buildable with [[phantom]]-style editing for the rendering axis and [[asap]]-style residual correction for the physics axis, and nobody has run it.

The second opening is tactile. Every deformable sim-to-real paper is vision-based, and for cloth and rope the contact signal is exactly what disambiguates the state. Combining this with your tactile world-model project is the natural move.
plan:
Pick one task with a clean metric — towel folding, or rope threading. Avoid anything where success is
  subjective.
Build the four-condition ablation. This is the contribution; the policy is incidental.

Add the residual-physics arm ([[asap]]-style delta model fitted to real rollouts) and report how much of
  the physics gap it closes.
Add tactile observation as a fifth condition, since for deformables it should help disproportionately.
Report the decomposition, not just the best number.
risks: Simulator choice determines the result. [[genesis]]'s multi-material support may or may not hold up; benchmark it against a rigid-only baseline before building on it.
Deformable state is hard to measure. Ground truth for "did the fold succeed" needs care.
Both gaps may be irreducible with current tools. That is a publishable negative result if the decomposition is clean.

The physics half via identification from real rollouts, on a cable.
Residual correction — the most likely tractable route for deformables.
Stress-guided reward: making 'do not break it' differentiable.
Multi-material simulation, if it holds up. Benchmark before trusting.
Editing real pixels instead of matching them — your rendering-axis tool.

transformer-robot.why:
A car that stands up and walks. The reason to take it seriously as research rather than as a stunt is that it is the cleanest instance of a problem the field has barely touched: control through a change of topology. Not a robot that reconfigures its joints, but one whose kinematic tree is genuinely different before and after — where the chassis becomes the torso and a structural panel becomes a limb.

It is also honest work. The robot either stands up and walks or it does not, and no benchmark choice can hide the answer.
transformer-robot.state:
First, the distinction that matters. The wheel-legged robots this gets confused with — [[x2n]], [[swheg]], [[reconfig-wheelleg]] — keep the same topology throughout: they are legged robots with wheels at the feet, and the "transformation" is a joint reconfiguration. [[x2n]] (April 2026) is the most advanced of these, with RL whole-body control spanning hybrid locomotion, reconfiguration and manipulation. Worth reading closely, but it is a different and easier problem than a car whose body opens into a humanoid.

The real car ↔ humanoid machines exist, and every one of them scripts the transformation. [[jdeite]] is the landmark: a 4 m rideable robot from BRAVE ROBOTICS, Asratec and Sansei that drives at 60 kph on wheels and walks as a biped, converting in about one minute under Asratec's V-Sido controller. The conversion is quasi-static and open-loop, and the bipedal walking is slow and statically stable. [[letrons]] converts a drivable BMW into a 4.5 m robot that articulates arms and fingers but does not walk — which tells you where the difficulty actually is. [[robosen]] is the most under-appreciated reference here: a consumer product with 34 servos that converts automatically between a walking biped and a vehicle at roughly half a metre, proving the mechanism is tractable once you stop trying to build it at four metres.

The modelling tool for a changing kinematic tree now exists. [[changing-morph-dyn]] gives closed-form, singularity-free whole-body Lagrangian dynamics for legged robots whose morphology changes — each limb modelled independently and reassembled according to the current configuration, so you do not re-derive the dynamics per mode. [[var-topology-truss]] is the formal treatment of planning when members change role, which is the abstract version of a panel becoming a limb.

One policy across changing bodies is a solved-ish architecture question. [[gcnt]] is a graph transformer that accepts an arbitrary module count and generalises zero-shot to unseen morphologies; [[morph-hypernet]] distils morphology-conditioned hypernetworks so one network emits weights for whatever body it is handed, which is cheaper at inference — and inference cost matters when the policy runs on the robot. [[getup-morphologies]] is the proof this works in practice: one policy recovering seven different humanoids, transferring zero-shot at ~86%.

Falling and getting up is now a real sub-field and you will need all of it. [[humanup]] is the reference getting-up result. [[unirelo]] unifies recovery and locomotion into one policy rather than bolting them together — directly relevant to counting policies. [[fall-safety]] does the under-studied half, falling well, from a few demonstrations. [[stablemimic]] handles structured post-fall behaviour when a tracking policy leaves its distribution, and [[kungfu-bot]] contributes a balance-challenging dynamic motion dataset with autonomous fall-resilient tracking.

And for actually building it: [[berkeley-humanoid-lite]] (printable, ~$5k, printed cycloidal gearboxes), [[toddlerbot]] (small, repairable, sim-fidelity-first), [[disney-bdx]] (expressive motion on a real biped), and [[mit-cheetah]] for the actuator argument that dominates everything.
threads: Topology change vs joint reconfiguration. [[jdeite]], [[letrons]], [[robosen]] on one side; [[x2n]], [[swheg]] on the other. Know which problem you are solving.
Dynamics of a changing kinematic tree. [[changing-morph-dyn]], [[var-topology-truss]], [[opt-legged-control]].
One policy, many bodies. [[gcnt]], [[morph-hypernet]], [[getup-morphologies]], [[cross-humanoid-wbc]].
Falling and recovering. [[humanup]], [[unirelo]], [[fall-safety]], [[stablemimic]], [[kungfu-bot]].
Compressing behaviours into few policies. [[hover]] and [[maskedmimic]] — masked training and distillation are how several behaviours fit in one network.
Buildable small platforms. [[berkeley-humanoid-lite]], [[toddlerbot]], [[robosen]], [[mit-cheetah]].
transformer-robot.gap:
The machines exist; the control does not. Every real car ↔ humanoid robot converts with a scripted, open-loop, quasi-static sequence — J-deite takes sixty seconds. Two claims follow, and the second is the one worth chasing.

1. Closed-loop, dynamic transformation. A morphology-conditioned policy that controls the robot continuously through the topology change: balance maintained across the transition, the contact set migrating from four wheels through multi-contact to two feet, and the manoeuvre abortable and reversible partway. Target under two seconds against J-deite's sixty. [[changing-morph-dyn]] gives you the model, [[gcnt]]/[[morph-hypernet]] give the policy architecture, and nobody has put them together on a topology-changing machine.

2. Transformation as a recovery primitive. This is the part nobody has. Every getting-up paper treats a fallen posture as something to escape by learning a get-up trajectory for it, and the long tail of postures is exactly where those policies fail. A transforming robot has a second option: fold into the wheeled form, right itself, unfold. That converts the morphology change from a feature into a controller primitive, and it may be dramatically more reliable than posture-specific get-up across the tail. Compare it head-to-head against [[humanup]]-style recovery on the same hardware and the same fallen-posture distribution. If it wins, it is a clean and slightly delightful result; if it loses, the failure analysis is still worth publishing.

And the systems question underneath both: the policy budget. Every paper here reports what its robot can do; none reports how many policies it took or what merging them costs. For a small robot with a small compute budget that is the binding constraint, and [[hover]]/[[maskedmimic]] give you the method to measure it.
plan:
Read [[jdeite]] and [[robosen]] before drawing anything, and be clear with yourself that you are solving
  the control problem, not the mechanism problem — the mechanism is demonstrated.

Build small. [[robosen]] scale (~0.5 m) or [[berkeley-humanoid-lite]] scale, printed, off-the-shelf quasi-direct-drive actuators. A transforming robot falls constantly during development and four metres of it falling is a research programme in itself.

Fix the actuator double-duty problem in the design phase: driving wants high speed and low torque,
  standing wants the opposite. Either two actuators (mass) or a transmission (complexity) — decide early,
  because it determines everything downstream. [[mit-cheetah]] is the reference.

Get driving and walking working as separate policies first in Isaac Lab ([[rudin2021]]). Do not attempt
  the transition until both endpoints are solid.

Model the transition with [[changing-morph-dyn]] and train the transformation policy with the morphology
  parameter in the observation, [[getup-morphologies]]-style. Reward: stay within the support polygon through
  the contact-set migration, and finish in under two seconds.

Headline experiment: drop the robot into N randomised fallen postures and compare a learned get-up policy against fold-to-wheeled-and-right-yourself. Report success rate, time and energy for each, and the postures where each one fails.
Systems result: distil the specialists into one masked policy ([[hover]]-style) and measure exactly what each behaviour loses. That is the number the field is missing.
risks: The mechanism eats the year. Transforming joints carry reversed structural loads and a printed version will break. Budget three revisions and keep a non-transforming fallback that still walks, so the learning work is never blocked on the hardware.

Sim-to-real across a changing kinematic chain. Contact and inertia both change mid-manoeuvre, which is where simulators are least trustworthy. [[asap]]-style delta-action correction is the escape hatch, and [[wheeled-payload]]'s real-to-sim equilibrium estimation is the closest precedent for a body whose plant changes.

Packaging. Everything must fold into a car silhouette, which leaves no room for conventional actuator placement. This is the constraint that makes the design genuinely hard and the reason [[robosen]]'s packaging is worth studying line by line.

It reads as a demo. Transforming robots are charismatic, which cuts both ways. The recovery-by-transformation comparison and the policy-budget measurement are what make it a paper rather than a video.

robot-dj.why:
Turntablism is an unusually good robotics benchmark hiding inside a fun idea. It demands continuous force regulation against a moving surface, bimanual coordination where the two hands have completely different jobs (one works the platter, one works the crossfader), timing precision in the tens of milliseconds, and — the property that makes it worth building — the task's own output is a dense, objective, real-time evaluation signal.

Every other contact-rich benchmark needs an external judge: did the peg seat, did the cloth fold. Here the robot's actions produce sound, the sound can be compared to a target, and that comparison is available at audio rate with no human and no instrumentation. That is rare enough to build a benchmark around.
robot-dj.state:
Audio as a robot modality is well established — and it is always used the same way. [[maniwav]] is closest to your setup: an ear-in-hand contact microphone on a UMI-style handheld gripper, collecting audio-visual demonstrations in the wild and learning policies directly from them. [[hearing-touch]] does audio-visual pretraining with piezo contact mics and reports the finding that matters here — sound helps most in the low-data regime and under texture change. [[sonicsense]] (Duke) puts a contact microphone in every fingertip of a four-finger hand and recovers material, contents and 3D shape from tapping and shaking. [[audio-vla]] folds contact audio into a VLA backbone. [[vibecheck]] goes active — inject a vibration and listen to the response rather than waiting for the task to make noise. [[miccheck]] shows the whole sensing stack can be off-the-shelf pin microphones for a few dollars.

Fusion has a reference study and a representation trick. [[see-hear-feel]] remains the cleanest account of when vision, touch and audio each actually contribute. [[robot-synesthesia]] contributes the idea worth copying: project the modalities into a shared 3D space rather than concatenating their feature vectors. [[av-contact]] estimates extrinsic contact — where the held object meets the world, not where the hand meets the object — from vision and sound together, which for a stylus riding a groove is the entire state estimation problem.

The music-side literature is where your evaluation comes from, and roboticists never read it. [[dj-mix-analysis]] (ISMIR 2020) aligns real DJ mixes back to their source tracks to recover cue points, transition lengths, mix segmentation and the musical edits the DJ made. It is the only body of work that quantifies what a DJ did rather than whether a listener enjoyed it. Alongside it sits the Turntablist Transcription Methodology (TTM, 2000) — a gridded staff notation for scratches encoding record position, hand motion and crossfader state, and the de-facto standard among turntablists. TTM is the piece that turns this from a demo into a benchmark, because it gives you a score: a written target the robot can be asked to perform and measured against.

Hardware for the contact side is ready. [[dexskin]] for conformable coverage, [[anyskin]] for sensors you can replace without recalibrating, [[doglove]] if you want force-feedback human demonstrations, and [[falcon]]'s external-force curriculum for the control problem of pushing against something that pushes back.

What does not exist anywhere: robot learning where audio is the objective. In every paper above, sound is an input used to infer a state that some other signal scores. Musical robotics has the objective — Shimon and the marimba-playing lineage at Georgia Tech — but those systems strike discrete notes under scripted or planned control, rather than modulating continuous friction against a moving platter.
threads: Contact microphones as sensors. [[sonicsense]], [[miccheck]], [[vibecheck]]. A piezo disc costs a dollar — the cheapest new modality you can add to a hand.
Policies learned from audio. [[maniwav]], [[hearing-touch]], [[audio-vla]].
Multimodal fusion. [[see-hear-feel]] for when each modality helps, [[robot-synesthesia]] for how to combine them, [[av-contact]] for extrinsic contact.
Force against a moving surface. [[falcon]]'s force curriculum, [[force-grasp-s2r]], and the contact-rich RL literature.
Evaluation from music information retrieval. [[dj-mix-analysis]], plus TTM notation and the beat tracking / onset detection literature. This is the half that makes it measurable.
In-the-wild capture with sound. [[maniwav]]'s ear-in-hand rig, worn by an actual DJ, generates exactly the demonstrations you need.
robot-dj.gap:
The novel claim is structural rather than incremental: turntablism is the first manipulation task where the reward and the observation are the same modality. The policy acts, the action makes sound, and the sound is simultaneously what it observes and what it is scored on. That buys three things no other contact-rich benchmark has:

  • No reward instrumentation. The blocker that kills most real-world RL projects — building a reliable automatic success detector — simply is not present. That connects this directly to your real-world RL harness idea: this is a task that can run unattended overnight.
  • A dense, continuous reward at audio rate rather than a sparse success bit at episode end.
  • An evaluation any human can judge instantly, which makes listening studies cheap and honest.

On top of that it forces three things the dexterity benchmarks avoid: regulating normal force against a moving surface with a real friction budget; timing where being 30 ms early is exactly as wrong as being 30 ms late; and bimanual asymmetry with a hard real-time coupling between the hands.

plan: Rig. Belt-drive turntable (torque you can fight without destroying it), dexterous hand with a [[sonicsense]]-style piezo in each fingertip, a [[miccheck]] pin mic on the tonearm, wrist F/T, and a wrist camera for platter angle. Take audio from the mixer line-out, never a room microphone — you want the signal the task produces, not the room's opinion of it.

Representation. Log-mel at 10–20 ms hop for the policy; keep the raw waveform for the reward. Fuse with vision and force via [[robot-synesthesia]]'s shared-space trick rather than feature concatenation, and pretrain the audio encoder [[hearing-touch]]-style on unlabelled scratching before any policy training.

Reward. Multi-resolution STFT distance to the target (borrowed from neural vocoders, because it is differentiable and perceptually reasonable), plus an onset-alignment term from onset detection, plus a force penalty and a stylus-skip penalty. Build and validate this first — everything downstream is standard, and this is the piece that is actually novel.

Method: three stages. (1) Human demonstrations with a [[maniwav]]-style ear-in-hand rig worn by a real DJ — scratch motions are highly stereotyped, so a few hundred should go far. (2) Behaviour cloning with a flow-matching action head ([[manflow]]) rather than diffusion, because the loop budget is ~20 ms and a denoising chain will not fit. (3) Residual RL on the real rig ([[pld]], [[hil-serl]]) against the spectral reward — which needs no human, so it can run unattended.
Curriculum. Baby scratch → forward/reverse → tear → chirp (crossfader cuts) → flare → transformer, then two-deck beat-matching, which adds tempo estimation and a second platter.

Ablations that make it a paper. audio-in-observation vs vision-only; audio-in-reward-only vs both; force sensing on/off; and the one that tests the actual claim — does having reward and observation in the same modality improve sample efficiency versus the identical task scored by an external judge?

metrics.title: What makes a good DJ — three tiers of metric

tiers.name: Tier 1 · Objective and automatic (per technique)
items: Onset timing error. Mean |Δt| between produced and target onsets, and the fraction landing within ±10 ms. Trained listeners reliably detect rhythmic error around 20 ms, so ±10 ms is the bar.
Beat / phase F-measure. Standard beat-tracking F-measure of the produced audio against the reference click — the MIR community's metric, directly reusable.
Spectral distance. Multi-resolution STFT loss against a reference performance of the same notated pattern. Doubles as the training reward.
Fréchet Audio Distance. Distributional, reference-free, against a corpus of human scratches — catches 'technically aligned but sounds wrong' in a way per-onset metrics cannot.
Platter velocity tracking. Variance of hand-imposed platter velocity during a held note. This is the pure motor-control number, isolated from musical judgement.
Crossfader gate accuracy. Fraction of cuts opening and closing inside the intended window — the bimanual-coordination number.
Damage rate. Stylus skips and excess-force events per minute. A policy that scores well and destroys records has not solved the task.

tiers.name: Tier 2 · Musical, from the turntablism literature
items: TTM score-following. The Turntablist Transcription Methodology gives a written notation for scratches (record position, hand, crossfader). Define a task suite as TTM scores, have the robot perform them, transcribe the output audio back to TTM, and score the edit distance. This is a clean, objective, musically meaningful benchmark that does not exist for robots and would be the paper's central artefact.

Technique taxonomy coverage. Report per-technique success across the standard vocabulary — baby, forward, chirp, tear, flare, crab, transformer, orbit — rather than one aggregate number. They stress different capabilities: chirp and transformer are crossfader-dominant, flare and crab are bimanual, tear is pure platter control.

Mix-level metrics. For the beat-matching half, [[dj-mix-analysis]]'s mix-to-track alignment recovers cue points, transition length and segmentation from a produced mix — giving objective measures of transition quality against how human DJs actually do it.
Tempo robustness. Hold the pattern, sweep the BPM. Where does it break? Human turntablists degrade gracefully; a policy overfit to one tempo will not.

tiers.name: Tier 3 · Human judgement (the only ground truth for 'good')
items: MUSHRA-style listening test. Robot performance against human DJs of varying skill and a hidden anchor, on the same notated pattern at the same tempo. This is the standard audio-quality protocol and it transfers directly.
Pairwise preference with expert DJs. Cheaper than MUSHRA and better suited to 'which of these two is better', which is the question that actually matters.
Turing test. Can turntablists tell robot from human above chance, per technique? Reporting the techniques where they cannot is a stronger result than any aggregate score.

Correlation study. Regress the Tier-1 automatic metrics against Tier-3 human preference. If spectral distance plus onset timing predicts expert preference well, you have contributed an automatic evaluator for the whole area — arguably more valuable than the policy.

risks: It reads as a novelty act. The defence is the benchmark framing — same-modality reward, force against a moving surface, millisecond timing, TTM score-following. Lead with that, not with the music.

Latency. Meaningful audio feedback means the whole perception-action loop must fit in roughly 20 ms. A diffusion head will not; use [[manflow]] or [[consistency-policy]], or run the reward off-policy.
Hardware wear. Styluses and records are consumables and a bad policy eats both quickly. Cheap cartridge, scratch-specific record, and a hard force ceiling below the policy in the control stack.

The reward is gameable. Spectral distance can be satisfied by scraping in a way that sounds roughly right and ruins the record. Keep the force penalty, the skip counter, and a human listening check in the evaluation — and report the gaming attempts you found, because they are interesting.

Musicians may disagree with the metric. Good turntablism has expressive timing that deliberately sits off the grid. That is why Tier 3 exists and why the correlation study matters — if your automatic metrics anti-correlate with expert preference, that is a finding, not a failure.
